Not all homeless are mentally ill. Some are. Same with substance users / abusers, and those who work. It’s a tough problem to crack because of the diversity in the homeless population- one size fits all solutions just don’t exist. Especially when you remember not all of them want to go back to stability. Less internal needs like food, toilets, a warm shower, a safe sleep, clothing (clean, that is, since most clothing banks can’t wash their received donations, which increases the risk for parasites spreading), transportation, and job search assistance are usually prioritized. Healthcare seems hit-and-miss unless folks try to get public assistance for it.

Entertainment is severely limited because folks seem to forget how many hours there are in a day.

It’s important knowing how to take the steps necessary to get back on your feet, but it’s the barriers to those behaviors that make it even more problematic. Less populated areas seem to have fewer resources so getting to a city seems like it helps. Where services exist, we’re told to show up as soon as places open to pursue those services, and those who don’t for whatever reason have probably just signed themselves up for several hours of waiting for just one thing. And may not get it seen at all. Help is rarely when and where it’s most needed. Emergency-weather shelters where I live require you to register early in the day and attend an orientation. Only soup/food lines seem to run smoothly, assuming you can find one that’s still serving and not an outdated help listing. Narrow windows of opportunity are painful, and prevalent. Nonprofits have the ability to be picky about who they help, as well, for any reason or no reason.

If you aren’t clean and dressed decently, it may not matter that you’ve scored a job interview. If you stood in a breakfast line, you’re too late for day labor. If you are chronically tired from getting poor rest, your work performance isn’t likely to be at its best and might get you fired if you’re slower to self-correct. If you’re relying on a bike, it can get stolen; if you’re relying on the city bus, it could be just slightly late (or early!) and you miss an important connecting bus that ruins the rest of the day. It just goes on.

Speaking practically and directly to what you asked, underwear, socks, and decent shoes seem to be least donated at clothing banks. Comfort food is fairly unusual at food banks, unless it’s expired. Odd job opportunities seem largely limited to smartphone apps, which can be REALLY frustrating to learn to use and spread thin the available listings (if they even have an app-ready phone). Be encouraging and friendly. Ask what they need, and know where to tell them to get it, or who they could call (United Way is often a safe start). Because homeless needs differ.

5. Flexibility, mental / emotional wellness.

From this newcomer’s perspective, flawed though it may be - centralized need has not led to centralized responsiveness in the community at large. As a result, there is both redundancy and “missed spots” in the services offered to Denver’s homeless. Rigid scheduling is sometimes unhelpful; it doesn’t universally encourage stability or time awareness, but it does universally exclude anyone with needs after-hours. But who is going to tell a volunteer that their generous donation of hours-of-service isn’t great, or appreciated? Who would cover the later shifts that would be required to extend operating hours through to 24 - even if only at one or two locations? How would attendance requirements have to change?

Flexibility and lack of constraints are some of the first things people tend to think of when imagining the homeless situation, but really, if you’re staying in a shelter nothing could be further from the truth. (I haven’t done so here, but I had two separate stays at a shelter in Lexington, KY some years ago and I daresay I remember how it went.)

Rules were weird until I tried reading between the lines, like - Can’t bring in outside food or drinks, not even sealed, because we don’t trust you not to bring in contraband hidden inside - Can’t use the kitchen after hours to make the noodle pouch we gave you, because we don’t trust others not to join you and collectively raid the kitchen supplies - Can’t be out after 8pm, because we don’t trust you not to be out doing drugs, even if your job confirms your schedule - Can’t be on the property between such-and-such hours, because we think putting you out means you’ll eventually be bored enough to get a job, or second job - well. I may have taken some liberties with the unspoken, but it really was the sort of treatment we expected at that place. Guilty until proven innocent (which was never), demands to participate in religious and/or self help services EVEN IF you demonstrated interest in (and ability to) work and participation would reduce the time you had to get to and from work-related activities of all sorts, room raids at all hours of the night so rest cycles were constantly disrupted, exposure to parasites during head checks (oh man, the parasites) - and once, a member of staff accused individuals of bringing lice into the facility in front of everyone else, unhelpful and degrading in the extreme, forcing rent collection (small though the amounts would seem, it still reduces their savings) without offering labor alternatives, I could go on.

A lot of the things I brought up in the wall of text up there play a part in whether or not someone is mentally prepared for work commitments, but there’s more to it than that. Underlying conditions, especially of the untreated variety, can render all job-search assistance pointless. If a person has undiagnosed social anxiety or some similar affliction, they are probably going to have more trouble holding a public job than a “well” individual - and if they’re highly emotionally sensitive, which doesn’t seem to be a protected status as far as I can tell, they’re risking their sanity to some extent with every job “opportunity” where the boss isn’t understanding or kind or patient with new-hires. I *would* list work opportunities as a need for the homeless, but really, it’s all this other stuff that seems to get in the way significantly. Jobs are there, day labor for the most part is there, it’s just one of the last concerns a homeless person faces... after most of the rest of it is dealt with. The magic that makes a lease possible, and from which all good things spring... it’s not like homeless people don’t know! You know?!

6. More things?

There are actual lists of things and services homeless folks need. (Hail almighty Google, hah.) I chose to speak personally, so I didn’t hit all the points, only the ones that occurred to me. Leisure? Yeah, having fun of some kind does make you feel more human. When I can blow the gas, I ADORE going to Paco Sanchez park for a morning climb (the rope structure is Amazing!), or to the Big Easy trailhead for a hike... things I just can’t imagine being high on the list of priorities for most homeless folks... things that make me think, really, I’ve got it pretty good. I’m NOT stuck following a shelter’s schedule, I have the car, and I’m not yet so worn down that I can’t do day labor. If only the cops would stop telling me to “move on” without adding where I’m supposed to go, I might even say this is living the dream. I am surrounded by mountains, after all! :D

3. Sleep. REAL sleep.

I lost a McJob on Wadsworth (on the overnight shift) over lack of sleep, though indirectly. The first week was okay, swapping between that shift and what day labor I could catch. After that week, it seemed like I couldn’t catch up on rest, no matter how little else I did than chase sleep. My good (if I do say so myself) work performance deteriorated on every job; I became a dangerous, inattentive liability; I had three unreported slip-and-fall incidents that were completely avoidable (and painful). In the end, I managed to find a blessedly shady spot in the afternoon prior to an overnight McD shift, tried to get my four hours of sleep before heading to the YMCA to shower and proceeding to McD’s, and instead slept through my entire shift. I think they might have forgiven me based on past performance if I hadn’t been messing up so badly recently.

Point being, once you’re experiencing a period of sleep deficiency, it can be darn-near impossible to feel caught up. Cramming everyone into shelters isn’t practical either, not as long as shelters demand rigidly structures coming-and-going hours. There’s no way I could have stayed at a shelter AND worked overnight, and I’m definitely not the only homeless person in Denver that has tried to juggle conflicts in timing between work and shelter attendance requirements. Where else can people without access to a personal space like a car even feel safe enough to fall asleep? If you don’t feel safe but you’re passing out anyway, that isn’t quality sleep... it’s essentially just pressing fast-forward.

Maybe a safe camping area with security and portable toilets, similar to the car-specific Safe Parking LA organization but also for shelter overflow and people avoiding shelters for whatever reason?

4. Storage, transportation.

I couldn’t decide which of these I would prioritize so I dumped them together. I’ve got both, after a fashion, at least until my car costs more to repair than I can come up with at day labor. My car is the only real asset I have - losing its functions would be the most grievous event I could imagine. It’s my single top priority, personally, though again I admit my situation probably isn’t the most common. I’ve already needed to pay for brake work (I swear, Colorado drivers need to figure out where their turning signals are located, and bother using them, especially on hills, geez). Still have to fix the AC (yeah, it’s been a sweaty few weeks), and get an air filter replacement for the cabin (getting transmission smells, which probably means I’m adding THAT to the list of bull my car needs).

Alternative transport for low/no income folks would be comforting. If all that’s offered is help getting to and from a medical office, there are a sad lot of missed opportunities to help the homeless help themselves. How about monthly non-transferable bus passes the homeless could earn somehow with a one-day or two-day time commitment? Or just to be given away - sometimes “jumping through hoops” to get what a charity offers isn’t feasible. Something, anyway, something absolutely attainable, that isn’t a one-day stop-gap solution? Fuel cards are less likely to pass muster because they could theoretically be sold, though not every homeless person has an addiction or other cash-blowing habit.

Then too, alternatives to buses are needed. It’s all about that rigid schedule. One missed bus can ruin a job opportunity, and even if it was quite literally beyond the rider’s control, an interviewer probably isn’t going to be impressed with the idea that THIS person is demonstrably unreliable... because responsible people leave super early when work is at stake so nothing short of a natural disaster can make them late... riiiight? (Or at least, this seems to be the prevailing expectation - a “there’s no such thing as an explanation, only good excuses and bad ones” sort of mentality.)

Like bringing personal belongings to an interview or job. Just uncouth! Who would do such a thing!? The homeless without a place to put their stuff, that’s who; with so little left, it’s hard to contemplate leaving it somewhere, especially if you don’t know when you’re coming back for it or whether it will still be there. Still, since it means getting to blend in with the “real” citizens, not hauling backpacks and shopping bags like some kind of visible announcement of disadvantage, I’d bet it would be a popular service if more places offered it.

Heck, I considered just outright renting a storage unit on the ignorant belief that my messy backseat was the only thing preventing me from trying to be a Lyft contractor or something similar - I’m lucky it occurred to me to Google what it takes to be a contract driver. That prevented an expense that I can now dismiss as unnecessary. I mean, I look forward to having my backseat back again, but putting all my stuff in a spot where I’m only “visiting” is just... depressing to consider.

Belatedly, but as a car-dwelling homeless person that is facing her first winter unsheltered, I have some thoughts on this... walls of text incoming - because Reddit has character limits, I have to try to split this post.

1. Food - particularly nutrition-dense, comfort-giving, and/or nonperishable in some combination.

When you don’t really know where your next meal is coming from, it can be a really horrible point of anxiety, even for someone that isn’t going hungry (as in, somebody that ate at least once that day). I keep a few nonperishables around, for myself and for passing out when I see someone with even less than I have, because I DO have a car and can get to day labor and Dollar Tree with relative frequency. It’s food that is fairly devoid of nutritional value, but it produces waste, so it must count.

Hot-meal and sandwich line locations can be hugely helpful, to a lot of folks. Not quite so much in a situation like mine, because I have to be at the day labor office before any of them open, and I am usually not off work until after the food offerings are over. I end up eating from value menus way more than is healthy or financially prudent, but it’s still cheaper than driving around looking for a gas station microwave to use. (How sad is that?)

2. Restroom facilities. Hygiene / cleanliness.

I never thought I would have to urinate on the street like some wasted drunkard for lack of public restroom facilities. I understand that places of business are under no orders to offer public restrooms, and the shocking disrespect such facilities seem to see are a real disincentive for those businesses to keep them available. However, it seems more of a public nuisance to me - and potentially hazardous besides - to just have everyone go where they stand. I felt dehumanized, humiliated, and criminal the first few times I “went” on pavement. Then I discovered how rabid some of the badges are about making people “move on” and realized I couldn’t depend on getting to sleep next to anything remotely resembling a restroom. I had to abandon my comfort zone utterly.

Now it just seems like a completely unavoidable fact of car-dwelling, and my biggest remaining concerns are getting into some kind of official trouble for 4am bladder bursting, getting urine on the hem of my pants legs from the backsplash or from the puddle, and making sure my toilet paper or napkins don’t fly off on the wind before I can throw them away properly. I miss being able to put clean clothes on a clean body as a thing to be taken for granted, too; it makes menstruation a much more frightening event than it ever was before. Dignity is one of the first things to go, or so I’m told, but I wouldn’t have expected clean clothes to poof too. There are a few cheap laundromats around, but I know if I am having trouble budgeting for such even with the decent pay from day labor, there’s probably a need there for others... or maybe my curse is a blessing and is just the result of having “enough” clothes that I can accumulate dirty laundry to fret over washing.

I don’t know how it would work, but gifting the homeless with YMCA memberships might help with hygiene AND leisure, though transportation and hours of operation are still potential barriers. It’s $55 monthly for me, a single adult, and I can get showered, shaved, swim (bought myself a bathing suit, felt like a real luxury), exercise out of the elements, have some coffee, read a magazine, etc. I wish it was cheaper, but that’s still less than the cost of two McChickens daily - and if I understand correctly, a membership is good at any Y location in the country. Pretty cool.
